issues.legal_issue: Reassessment is invalid when the assessee disclosed the primary facts and the statutory basis for reopening requires an omission or failure by the assessee to disclose those facts.
material_facts: The reassessment proceedings concerned income-tax years for which the original assessments had been made.
The assessee had provided the lease agreement, including its terms, to the tax officer during the original assessments.

The tax officer knew of the dispute between the assessee, the state government and the Union concerning the royalty and tax liability, and had received an injunction relating to assessment proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The reassessments based on the alleged failure to disclose material facts were invalid because the assessee had disclosed the primary facts and was not required to draw the tax officer’s attention to a particular clause or inference.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, reopening requires reason to believe both that income escaped assessment and that the escape resulted from the assessee’s omission or failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts. The disclosure duty concerns primary facts, not the obligation to point out particular parts of documents or the inferences to be drawn from them. The Court relied on Calcutta Discount Co. Ltd. v. ITO (41 ITR 191).

predicates.income_tax_reassessment_proceeding: The tax authority reopened an earlier income-tax assessment.
predicates.primary_facts_disclosed: The assessee provided the primary documents and facts relevant to the assessment to the tax officer.
predicates.tax_officer_knew_relevant_dispute: The tax officer knew of the dispute bearing on how the disclosed facts related to the assessment.

issues.definition: When an income-tax reassessment follows disclosure of the primary facts and the tax officer knew of the relevant dispute, the reassessment is invalid if it depends on an alleged failure to disclose those facts.

issues.legal_issue: A reassessment initiated on one statutory ground may be sustained on an alternative ground when that ground’s requirements are met, including its time limit and the tax officer’s possession of information indicating escaped assessment.
material_facts: The reassessments for three assessment years had been initiated under the provision requiring an assessee’s failure to disclose material facts.
Those proceedings were initiated within the shorter time limit applicable to the alternative reopening ground.

The original assessments had allowed deduction of the entire royalty payment, including the component paid in lieu of tax; the tax officer later had information indicating that income had been under-assessed.
The information could be derived from the assessment record, provided its existence and implications were recognized.
issues.conclusion: Although the reassessments could not stand on the ground on which they had been initiated, they could be sustained on the alternative ground because its requirements were met.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, permits reopening within its time limit where the tax officer, in consequence of information in his possession, has reason to believe income escaped assessment, even without an omission or failure by the assessee. Information may come from the assessment record itself when its existence is realized and its implications recognized. The Court relied on Salem Provident Fund Society Ltd. v. CIT (42 ITR 547), United Mercantile Co. Ltd. v. CIT (64 ITR 218), and Anandji Haridas & Co. v. S.P. Kasture (AIR 1968 SC 565), and held that the contrary view in Raghubar Dayal Ram Kishan v. CIT (63 ITR 572) was not good law.

rule.if: income_tax_reassessment_proceeding and reassessment_started_on_another_ground and within_applicable_reopening_limit and information_indicated_escaped_assessment

predicates.income_tax_reassessment_proceeding: The tax authority reopened an earlier income-tax assessment.
predicates.reassessment_started_on_another_ground: The tax authority initiated reopening on a ground different from the alternative ground later relied on to sustain it.
predicates.within_applicable_reopening_limit: The reopening occurred within the time limit applicable to the alternative ground.
predicates.information_indicated_escaped_assessment: Information in the tax officer’s possession, including information recognized from the assessment record, indicated that income had escaped assessment.

issues.definition: An income-tax reassessment initiated on one ground may be sustained on an alternative ground when it is within that ground’s time limit and information in the tax officer’s possession indicates escaped assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to penal interest imposed in an assessment order may be raised in an appeal against the tax assessment, but no separate appeal lies against the interest levy itself.
material_facts: The dispute concerned penal interest calculated and charged under section 18A(6) or section 18A(8) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
The interest was levied in the assessment order, and the assessee objected to it in an appeal against that assessment.
The High Court had not determined the relevant facts or the consequential relief, so the Supreme Court remitted that aspect for appropriate orders.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that there is no separate appeal against an order levying the interest, but the assessee may challenge liability to pay it in an appeal against the assessment order; the matter was remitted for the High Court to apply that rule to the facts.
issues.legal_principle: The Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, provided no specific right of appeal against an order levying interest. Where interest is levied by the assessment order, the assessee may contest liability to pay it in an appeal against that assessment, including while denying liability to be assessed. The Court relied on Pt. Deo Sharma v. CIT (23 ITR 226), Boddu Seetharmaswamy v. CIT (28 ITR 156), South India Flour Mills Ltd. v. CBDT (70 ITR 863), National Products v. CIT (108 ITR 935), CIT v. Sharma Construction Co. (100 ITR 603), K.B. Stores v. CIT (103 ITR 505), and Keshardeo Shrinivas Morarka v. CIT (48 ITR 404).

predicates.income_tax_assessment_appeal: The assessee appealed against an income-tax assessment order.
predicates.penal_interest_imposed_in_assessment_ord: The assessment order itself imposed penal interest.

issues.definition: When an assessee appeals an income-tax assessment and that order imposes penal interest, the assessee may challenge liability for the interest in that assessment appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Whether an amount paid as excess royalty in lieu of tax qualifies for credit against the assessee’s tax liability requires reconsideration where the effect of a court order directing payment of that amount to the taxing authority was not assessed.
material_facts: The assessee sought credit for the portion of excess royalty said to have been paid in lieu of income-tax and other taxes.
A court decree directed the state government to pay the Union an amount out of the excess royalty in respect of tax assessed and demanded from the assessee.
The High Court had rejected the credit claim without considering the decree’s effect, and it was unclear whether the relevant materials were before it.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to decide the credit question on the available record and remitted it to the High Court for fresh consideration in light of the stated facts.
issues.legal_principle: The Court did not decide the substantive entitlement to credit. It held that the question required reconsideration if the relevant materials were available to the High Court, including the decree directing payment to the Union, and remitted the matter for that consideration.

predicates.tax_credit_reference_issue: A question in a tax reference concerns whether an amount paid in connection with the assessee’s tax liability qualifies for credit.
predicates.court_order_directed_tax_payment_from_ro: A court order directed a government holding royalty proceeds to pay an amount from those proceeds to the taxing authority for tax assessed or demanded from the assessee.
predicates.effect_of_order_not_considered: The reviewing court had not assessed the effect of that payment direction on the credit question.

issues.definition: When a tax-credit reference involves a court-directed payment of royalty proceeds toward the assessee’s taxes and the effect of that direction was not considered, the credit issue is remitted for fresh consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Whether excess royalty is a deductible business expense requires reconsideration where the effect of the court-ordered payment of a tax component and other relevant materials was not assessed.
material_facts: The assessee claimed a deduction for royalty paid above the minimum amount under its lease.
The excess royalty was described as including an amount in lieu of income-tax and other taxes, as well as a remaining amount after that component.

The High Court treated the tax-equivalent component as non-deductible and the remaining amount as deductible, but the Supreme Court noted that relevant materials, including the decree directing payment to the Union and the asserted relevance of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, had not been considered.
The Supreme Court also noted an earlier decision involving the same assessee and different assessment years, when there was no income-tax law in the former state.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to decide the deduction question on the available record and remitted it to the High Court for fresh consideration in light of the stated facts and materials.
issues.legal_principle: The Court made no final ruling on the deductibility of the excess royalty. It directed the High Court to reconsider the question in light of the relevant facts and materials, including the court decree, the asserted application of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and the earlier decision concerning different years and a different tax-law context.

predicates.business_expense_deduction_reference_iss: A question in a tax reference concerns whether a payment connected with business is deductible as an expense.
predicates.excess_royalty_included_tax_component: The claimed expense included excess royalty described in part as being paid in lieu of the assessee’s taxes.
predicates.relevant_materials_not_considered: The reviewing court had not considered materials bearing on the character, payment, or deductibility of the claimed expense.

issues.definition: When a deduction reference concerns excess royalty including a tax component and relevant materials about the payment were not considered, the deduction issue is remitted for fresh consideration.
